Handle malformed or untrusted input

Source: vignettes/articles/untrusted-input.Rmd
untrusted-input.Rmd
library(zujson)

This guide is for code that parses a body it did not write: a response from a service, a file a user uploaded. It shows how to catch a failure, how to tell one kind from another, and which limits stop a hostile document from exhausting the C stack or memory. It assumes you have read vignette("zujson").

Catch every failure with one handler

Every condition the package raises inherits from zujson_error. Wrap the call once, and nothing zujson raises escapes as a bare error:

parse_or_null <- function(x) {
  tryCatch(json_parse(x), zujson_error = function(e) NULL)
}

parse_or_null('{"ok": true}')
#> $ok
#> [1] TRUE
parse_or_null("{bad")
#> NULL

Tell the failures apart

In front of zujson_error sits a class that says what went wrong. Handle the ones you can act on, and leave the rest to the general handler.

Class Raised when
zujson_parse_error the input is not JSON, or is JSON that R cannot hold
zujson_depth_error nesting goes past zujson_info()$max_depth levels
zujson_limit_error data_frame = TRUE would build more than zujson_info()$max_df_cells cells
zujson_io_error json_parse_file() cannot read the file
zujson_write_error a value cannot be written, such as a date outside years 0000 to 9999
zujson_unsupported_type an R type has no JSON form, such as a complex or raw vector
zujson_arg_error an argument is of the wrong type or length

The class comes first in class(e), and the message says where in the input the problem is:

e <- tryCatch(json_parse('{"a": }'), zujson_error = function(e) e)
class(e)
#> [1] "zujson_parse_error" "zujson_error"       "error"             
#> [4] "condition"
conditionMessage(e)
#> [1] "invalid JSON at byte 6: unexpected character, expected a JSON value"

For NDJSON the message names the line, since a byte offset into ten thousand records helps nobody:

json_parse_ndjson('{"id": 1}\n{"id": \n{"id": 3}\n')
#> Error:
#> ! invalid JSON on line 2 at byte 7 of that line: unexpected end of data

Do not rely on validating first

json_validate() answers “is this JSON?”. That is nearly, but not exactly, “will json_parse() succeed?”. Two kinds of document are valid JSON and still cannot become R values. The first is nesting deeper than the limit:

deep <- paste0(strrep("[", 1500), strrep("]", 1500))

json_validate(deep)
#> [1] TRUE
class(tryCatch(json_parse(deep), zujson_error = function(e) e))[1]
#> [1] "zujson_depth_error"

The second is a string R cannot hold, such as one with an escaped NUL:

nul <- '["a\\u0000b"]'

json_validate(nul)
#> [1] TRUE
class(tryCatch(json_parse(nul), zujson_error = function(e) e))[1]
#> [1] "zujson_parse_error"

So code that must not fail handles the condition from json_parse(). Use json_validate() when the yes or no is all you need. ?json_validate gives the reasoning for both cases.

The limits

zujson_info() reports the two limits in force, with the package and yyjson versions:

str(zujson_info())
#> List of 4
#>  $ zujson      : chr "0.1.1"
#>  $ yyjson      : chr "0.12.0"
#>  $ max_depth   : int 1000
#>  $ max_df_cells: num 5e+07

Depth. Building the R value is recursive, so nesting is capped at max_depth levels and a deeper document raises zujson_depth_error instead of overflowing the C stack. The cap is compiled in. json_validate() does not apply it, because the reader underneath is iterative and RFC 8259 leaves the limit to the implementation.

Data frame cells. A data frame is rectangular, so records that share no keys ask for one cell per record, per record: the size grows with the square of the body. max_df_cells bounds the total for one document. Here a limit of 10 cells refuses three records that share no keys:

withr::with_options(list(zujson.max_df_cells = 10), {
  json_parse('[{"a":1,"b":1},{"c":1,"d":1},{"e":1,"f":1}]', data_frame = TRUE)
})
#> Error:
#> ! a data frame of 3 records x 4 columns needs more than the 10 cells left of the document's 10 cell limit

Set options(zujson.max_df_cells = ) to raise or lower it for the session.

Text must be UTF-8

Every string zujson returns is marked UTF-8, and that mark is true because yyjson checked the bytes. Input that is not valid UTF-8 is refused, not repaired:

latin1 <- as.raw(c(0x22, 0xE9, 0x22)) # "é" in Latin-1, between quotes
json_validate(latin1)
#> [1] FALSE

Convert such input with iconv() before parsing. A leading UTF-8 byte order mark is skipped and not refused, since real services send one.
